passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antioxidant, Compound X, on the oxidative stress response in cultured human fibroblasts. Cells were exposed to 0, 10, 25, 50, and 100 µM of Compound X for 24 hours. After treatment, intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were quantified using a fluorescent probe, and cell viability was assessed via an MTT assay. Additionally, the expression of the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) was measured by quantitative PCR. The following table summarizes the mean ROS fluorescence intensity (arbitrary units) and percent cell viability relative to untreated controls for each concentration.
stem: Which concentration of Compound X resulted in the lowest ROS fluorescence intensity?
explanation: The 100 µM concentration gave the lowest ROS fluorescence (110 AU) versus 120 AU at 50 µM, 140 at 25 µM and 170 at 10 µM.
trap: Option C (50 µM) is close, but ROS keeps falling slightly at 100 µM, though with reduced viability (88%).

stem: Why is the cell viability measurement important for interpreting the fall in ROS?

options.A: A lower ROS signal could partly reflect fewer living cells, so viability shows whether the ROS decrease is due to cell loss.
options.B: Viability shows that Compound X is non-toxic at every concentration tested.
options.C: Viability measures SOD2 expression in the treated cells.
options.D: Viability is the independent variable that the researchers manipulated.

explanation: Correct: A) If cells die, the ROS signal can fall for reasons unrelated to antioxidant activity, so viability helps interpret the ROS data. Why the others are wrong: B) Viability fell to 88% at 100 µM, so the compound is not shown to be non-toxic. C) SOD2 expression was measured by quantitative PCR, not by the MTT assay. D) Concentration, not viability, was the manipulated variable.
trap: Reading the viability column as proof of no toxicity, when it fell steadily to 88% at 100 µM.

stem: If the mean ROS intensity at 50 µM is 120 units and at 0 µM is 200 units, what percent reduction in ROS does 50 µM Compound X produce?
trap: Reporting the remaining fraction (120/200 = 60%) instead of the 40% reduction.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the table?

options.A: ROS was lower than the untreated value at every concentration of Compound X tested.
options.B: Cell viability declined as the concentration increased.
options.C: SOD2 fold change rose with each higher concentration.
options.D: ROS at 100 µM was less than half of the untreated value.

explanation: Correct: D) ROS at 100 µM (110 AU) is 55% of the untreated 200 AU, a 45% reduction, not more than half. Why the others are wrong: A) 170, 140, 120 and 110 are all below 200. B) Viability was 100, 95, 92, 90 and 88%. C) SOD2 fold change was 1, 1.1, 1.3, 1.5 and 1.7.
trap: Rounding the fall from 200 to 110 AU to a halving; the actual reduction is 45%, not more than 50%.

stem: By what percent did SOD2 expression at 100 µM exceed that of untreated cells?
explanation: Correct: A) A fold change of 1.7 means 70% above the untreated value of 1.0. Why the others are wrong: B) 170% treats the fold change as the percent increase. C) 1.7% misreads the fold change as a percent. D) 41% is the fall from 1.7 back to 1.0 ((1.7 - 1.0)/1.7), not the rise above untreated.
trap: Reporting the fold change as a percent increase (170%) instead of subtracting the 1.0 baseline.
